info.title: proof.holdings API
info.description:
**Multi-Surface Proof of Control**

Cryptographic proofs of digital asset control. proof.holdings issues signed JWT proofs that a user controls a digital asset (phone, email, domain, social, wallet) by completing a challenge from that asset. Proofs are offline-verifiable using the public keys published at `/.well-known/jwks.json` (ES256).

## Core Concepts

- **Verification**: A challenge-response flow to prove control of an asset
- **Proof Token**: Signed JWT issued after successful verification (ES256)
- **JWKS**: Public keys for offline verification at `/.well-known/jwks.json`

## Authentication

Most endpoints require API key authentication via Bearer token:
```
Authorization: Bearer pk_live_...
```

Dashboard endpoints use JWT authentication via httpOnly cookies.

## Rate Limits

All authenticated endpoints include rate limit headers:
- `X-RateLimit-Limit`: Maximum requests per window
- `X-RateLimit-Remaining`: Requests remaining in current window
- `X-RateLimit-Reset`: Unix timestamp when window resets

## The 7 Proofs

proof.holdings is built around seven verification primitives. Four are live today; three are coming soon. This API exposes endpoints for the live primitives only.

1. **Proof of Control** (live) — verify control of a phone, email, domain, social account, or wallet. Endpoints: `/api/v1/verifications`, `/api/v1/verification-requests`.
2. **Proof of Delegation** (live) — a control-proven domain authorizes a typed url/purl artifact for a set of capability scopes, with an independently revocable signed token. The attestation is that the domain's controller authorized the artifact — nothing more. Endpoints: `/api/v1/delegations`.
3. **Proof of Action** (live) — human-in-the-loop approval for irreversible actions, cryptographically signed; authorizations are its consent layer. Endpoints: `/api/v1/hitl`, `/api/v1/confirmations`, `/api/v1/authorizations`.
4. **Proof of Me** (live) — anti-impersonation reverse verification via trusted Circle members. Endpoints: `/api/v1/circles`, `/api/v1/identity-challenges`.
5. **Proof of Agreement** (coming soon) — continuous witnessing for group conversations; no API endpoints yet.
6. **Proof of Development** (coming soon) — verifiable development provenance via the team.management integration; no API endpoints yet.
7. **Proof of Enforcement** (coming soon) — proof that mandated processes actually ran; no API endpoints yet.

Delegation-specific reasons: `unknown_delegation` (no registry record — delegations are minted fail-closed, so this is invalid, not merely unresolvable), `status_unavailable`, and `identifier_unverifiable` when an `identifier` binding is requested for a delegation.

is_expiring_soon.description: Whether this request is close enough to `expires_at` to act on — and the WINDOW depends on which side of the request is reading, so one row can honestly answer differently on two surfaces. Read `next_action.role` to know which answer you have. For a `requester` the window is the lesser of 24h and HALF the request's own lifetime, so a just-created short-lived request is NOT "expiring soon" (advising a reminder before the recipient has had any time is the case this excludes). For a `recipient` the window is a flat 24h, because they already hold the link and what matters is the deadline itself.

BOTH `is_expiring_soon` and `next_action` are role-aware — `next_action.role` says which side this envelope was computed for, and the two fields are consistent within it. Present only on authenticated owner/requester and recipient responses; absent on public/third-party surfaces.

status.description: The one status every read reports. `pending` — waiting for the person being checked; `confirmed` — they confirmed; `denied` — they denied; `cancelled` — whoever started the check withdrew it; `failed` — the check could not be delivered; `expired` — nobody answered in time; `revoked` / `suspended` — the confirmation's proof was revoked or suspended (`POST /proofs/{proof_id}/revoke` or `/suspend`; revoking a denial's proof leaves it `denied`), or — `revoked` only — the member being checked was removed from the Circle while the check was still pending, which leaves `proof_id` null. Removing a member is not guaranteed to revoke a confirmation they already gave; revoke that one by its `proof_id`. A proof that merely reached its own expiry still reads `confirmed`; whether its token is still valid is `POST /proofs/validate`'s answer.

TwoFAActionType.description: Action type requiring 2FA. Destructive actions (api_key_*, account_delete, account_delete_cancel, phone_remove, email_remove, domain_remove, profile_delete, master_key_change, hitl_key_rotate, revocation_bulk, delegation_lifecycle) are capped at 5 min TTL and forced single-use by server policy. `revocation_bulk` is the ONE action type for every proof revocation by the owner — phone, email or domain, one proof or a batch of up to 25, from the assets routes or a signed-in call on the proofs API; a grant is bound to the `targets` named at start and is refused for any other ids. `domain_remove` gates `DELETE /me/domains/{id}`, `profile_delete` gates `DELETE /me/profiles/{profileId}` for a session, `account_delete` gates scheduling the account deletion and `account_delete_cancel` gates cancelling it; each takes the single target id as its one `targets` entry. Configuration scopes (settings_write, profile_update, templates_write, webhook_write) allow up to 24h TTL with caller-chosen single_use. `master_key_change` gates a change of the HITL account encryption password. `hitl_key_rotate` gates a JWT dashboard session replacing the encryption keypair (a new `kid`) of an active HITL config — an API-key caller is unaffected, and the owner is emailed about every rotation from either path. `delegation_lifecycle` gates a JWT dashboard session revoking, suspending, or unsuspending a delegation (`ph_dlg_*` handle) — an API-key caller is unaffected, gated instead by the `delegations:write` scope. `phone_add` / `email_add` are preserved for backwards-compat with existing dashboard flows but no longer gate any backend route — the add-phone / add-email flows self-authenticate via reverse-OTP / OTP verification. `api_key_view` is reserved for UI surfaces that re-reveal an API key secret; `webhook_write` is reserved for future per-resource webhook mutations.

targets.description: The ids this step-up is for (1-25): asset ids for the assets routes, `ph_ctl_*` handles for the proofs API, the domain / profile / account id for a single-target action. The grant is bound to a digest of exactly these ids and the gated route refuses it with `2fa_required` (`reason: target_mismatch`) when the request names different ids. Omit for an untargeted action such as settings_write.

post.description:
Start a new verification challenge for an asset.

The `challenge` object withholds the completion material for the pairs whose code we deliver out-of-band — `type: email`, and `type: domain` with `channel: email`. For those the code and the magic link are absent by design: the delivery to the address IS what the proof rests on, so a caller holding the code would prove nothing by submitting it back. Every other pair keeps its code, because the caller has to relay it (phone) or publish it (the TXT record or well-known file for a domain).

503.description: `challenge_delivery_failed` — the challenge could not be delivered to the party being verified (email service unavailable, or the send reported failure). Applies to the two mailed pairs only. NO verification is created: the row is deleted, because the create response withholds the code for these pairs and a caller holding neither the mail nor the code has no way to complete it. Nothing is billed — a proof is billed when one is issued, and an undelivered challenge never reaches that point. Retry.

post.description: Validate a JWT proof token. Public endpoint — no authentication required. Can also be done offline using JWKS.

Revoke a proof token, making it invalid. Accepts the public proof handle (`ph_ctl_<32 hex>` or `ph_dlg_<32 hex>`) or a verification id — the same addresses the status, suspend and unsuspend routes take. Revoking a PROOF does not withdraw the asset, consent or delegation it is about: those have their own surfaces. The revocation reaches the registry row, `GET /proofs/{id}/status`, `POST /proofs/validate`, the revocation list and the Token Status List. One difference between the two addresses: by verification id a proof whose verification is not `verified` answers `not_verified`, while by handle it is revoked anyway — the registry row is live and would otherwise keep validating — leaving the verification in whatever state it really ended in. Reachable with an API key (`proofs:write`) or a dashboard session cookie; the scope binds API-key callers only. A CONTROL proof — a domain proof delegations can hang off (`ph_ctl_*` of a domain asset or verification, or a domain verification id) — takes the gated path (h-implement-proper-deletion, DOM-3): for a domain the account OWNS the whole-domain cascade runs (every proof of the domain and every delegation issued from it revoked, the domain demoted to `reverification_required` with its DNS challenge rotated — the same act as `DELETE /me/assets/{id}` on the domain asset); for a bare verification of somebody else's domain only that proof and the delegations anchored on it are revoked, sibling verifications stay live. The body then carries `principal`, `owned_domain`, `domain_status` and `delegations_revoked`. A repeat answers 200 while something was left to re-drive (a delegation still live under a revoked proof), else `400 already_revoked` — decided before any step-up code is spent. A handle revoked BEFORE the domain was proven again answers `400 already_revoked` and never reaches the new proof: revoke that one by its own handle. An API key revoking a control proof, or one of the account's own phone or email proofs, has the act recorded for the hourly owner digest (one digest per key).

400.description: Already revoked, not in a revocable state, or a revocation reason this proof type does not accept. `already_revoked` applies to a PROOF only: a repeat revoke of a DELEGATION handle (`ph_dlg_*`) answers 200 with the stored revocation instead, matching `POST /delegations/{id}/revoke`, whose contract has always advertised idempotency. The proof code stays as it is because it is published and read by integrators

403.description: For an API-key caller, acting on a delegation handle (`ph_dlg_*`) additionally requires the `delegations:write` scope, so it keeps the gate its own route puts on it (`insufficient_scope`). The same rule covers suspend and unsuspend for that handle: a pause takes the delegation offline for every verifier while it holds, which is what a revocation does, and being reversible bounds only the cost of putting it back. For a JWT dashboard session (which carries no scope), the same act instead requires a live `delegation_lifecycle` 2FA step-up grant (`403 2fa_required` — start one via `POST /me/2fa/start` with `action_type: delegation_lifecycle`), gated identically for revoke, suspend and unsuspend. For a CONTROL proof (a domain proof): an API key needs `delegations:write` as well while the act reaches live delegations — for revoke, suspend and unsuspend alike, since a pause hides the delegations exactly as a revocation does; a revoke of a domain the account OWNS reaches every live delegation of the domain, whichever of its handles was named — and the `insufficient_scope` body names `missing_scope` and `live_delegations`; a session needs, for REVOKE only, a consumed single-use `revocation_bulk` step-up grant bound to the id it sent (`2fa_required`; `reason: target_mismatch` when the grant names other ids) — the same code the dashboard's own routes demand, so this is not a 2FA-free address for the permanent cascade. A pause needs no step-up. A session revoking one of the account's OWN phone or email proofs (an asset proof, by its `ph_ctl_*` handle) needs the same `revocation_bulk` grant bound to that handle; a proof that is already revoked answers `400 already_revoked` without one, and an API key keeps its `proofs:write` rule.

get.description: Get signed list of revoked proofs for offline verification. When `has_more` is true the list was truncated — re-baseline and prefer the Token Status List (`status_list_uri`), which never truncates and also covers suspension.

The IETF Token Status List (draft-ietf-oauth-status-list) for all proofs. Public endpoint — no authentication. A schema-1.3 proof token carries `status.status_list.{idx, uri}`; fetch this list, verify its signature via JWKS, DEFLATE-decompress `status_list.lst` (base64url) and read the 2-bit value at your token's `idx`: 0 valid, 1 revoked, 2 suspended. The shared bit array reveals nothing about which entry was read (herd privacy), and unlike the revocation list it never truncates and can retract: an unsuspended proof's bit flips back to 0. Every slot the issuer hands out is inside the published array from the next fetch onward, and a revocation or suspension of the proof ITSELF reaches this channel within one minute (the advertised `ttl` plus the issuer's own rebuild interval); the point lookups answer immediately. One limit is deliberate: each entry carries its own row status, so a DELEGATION whose underlying domain control proof was revoked keeps a 0 (valid) bit here — that cascade is resolved at read time and only `POST /api/v1/proofs/validate` reports it.

post.description: Reversibly pause a proof (m-proof-status-list). A suspended proof answers invalid on validation and carries status-list bit 2, but unlike revocation the owner can lift it with the unsuspend endpoint. Only an active proof can be suspended. Accepts a public proof handle (`ph_ctl_<32 hex>` or `ph_dlg_<32 hex>`) or a verification id — the same addresses the status and revoke routes take. Reachable with an API key (`proofs:write`) or a dashboard session cookie; the scope binds API-key callers only. Suspending a DELEGATION handle (`ph_dlg_*`) additionally requires `delegations:write`, exactly as revoking one does: while the pause holds, every verifier rejects that delegation, which is what a revocation produces, and reversibility bounds the cost of restoring it rather than the reach of the act.

post.description:
Create a new passwordless auth session (login). Returns a deep link and QR code for the selected channel. Rate limited: 15 requests per minute per IP.

The email channel additionally honours the account-bootstrap decline cooldown: if the owner of the address used the "this wasn't me" link on a recent message from us, this endpoint answers 429 `identity_declined` for an hour. That covers sign-in mail as well, so a client should offer the other channels (Telegram, WhatsApp, SMS) rather than retrying.

No credential is required. A client that DOES present an API key (`Authorization: Bearer pk_…`) — an MCP connection signing in from inside — has it checked: a key the API no longer accepts (unknown, revoked, expired) is refused with 401 `invalid_api_key` before anything is stored or sent, so a connection whose key was revoked cannot sign back in to the account. A live presented key is recorded on the session, and the user session issued when the sign-in completes is BOUND to it: revoking that key by any path ends the session, and it cannot be refreshed once the key is revoked or expired. If the key is revoked before the person completes the sign-in, no session is issued at all.

ON THE EMAIL CHANNEL A 201 MEANS THE MAIL WAS ACCEPTED FOR DELIVERY. The code and the magic link travel in that message and are returned by nothing, so a session created after a failed send could never be completed — if delivery fails, this endpoint answers 503 `challenge_delivery_failed` and the session is discarded rather than returning a session to poll. Do not look for an `email_sent: false` to decide whether to tell someone to check their inbox: on this route a 201 already carries that answer. A field of that name DOES mean something elsewhere — `POST /api/v1/accounts` (AccountSessionResponse) and `POST /api/v1/accounts/{id}/send` (its own response shape) split creating a session from mailing it, and report a withheld or failed send that way — but those are different endpoints. This one still carries `email_sent` on an email-channel 201, where it is ALWAYS `true` (a failed send never reaches a 201), and it never returns `email_error` at all. Note that `email_sent` is NOT part of the declared 201 schema below: `AuthSessionResponse` is shared with the session-poll and submit operations, which return no such field, so it is documented here rather than declared there — a generated client type for this response will not carry it.

503.description: Either `identity_check_unavailable` — the decline check could not be completed, so the request is refused rather than allowed through — or, on the email channel, `challenge_delivery_failed`: the verification email could not be sent, so no session was created. Retry shortly, or offer another channel. A third code, `email_service_unavailable`, means no mail provider is configured at all.

post.description:
Create an account-bootstrap session for agent-driven onboarding. Public endpoint (rate limited: 15/min per IP, plus a per-identity budget of 3/hour for the email and SMS channels that no amount of IP rotation avoids).

The session is ALWAYS tagged `type="account_creation"`. It does NOT branch on whether the submitted identity already maps to a User — the response is uniform by design, because a differing shape or timing would answer "does this address have an account here?" to anyone who asks. Completing verification transparently creates a User when none exists or signs the existing one in; an agent that needs to tell those apart calls GET /auth/me afterwards and reads `created_at`.

THE EMAIL CHANNEL SENDS NOTHING HERE (`email_sent: false`, `send_required: true`). Delivering a message from our domain to an address nobody has proven is a separate, explicit act: POST /api/v1/accounts/{id}/send. The other channels are inbound — the user messages us (reverse OTP) — so nothing is dispatched to them at all.

No credential is required. A client that DOES present an API key (`Authorization: Bearer pk_…`) has it checked: a key the API no longer accepts is refused with 401 `invalid_api_key` before anything is stored, and a live one is recorded so the session issued on completion is BOUND to it — revoking the key by any path ends that session.

post.description:
Deliver the verification email that POST /api/v1/accounts deliberately withheld. Public endpoint — the session id is the bearer secret, the same model as the poll route.

One session sends at most one message. The material backing the send is claimed atomically when the send is ATTEMPTED — so two concurrent calls cannot both deliver — and a failed delivery hands it back, returning `email_sent: false` so the call can be retried. A repeat after a delivered send answers 410.

This is not an anti-abuse measure and does not claim to be one: whoever is willing to make two requests is not stopped by it. Volume is bounded by the per-identity budget on the create call and by the recipient's own decline link. What the split removes is the case where creating a session and mailing a stranger were the same act.

The signed-in owner needs a consumed single-use `account_delete` step-up grant whose one target is the account's own id (`403 2fa_required`; `reason: target_mismatch` when the grant names other ids); an API key answers `403 owner_session_required`. Proofs of decisions already made, and proofs issued to others, stay valid. On the date: billing is settled first (an unpaid final invoice puts the deletion `on_hold` with a Pay-invoice link rather than deleting past it), then everything owned is deleted and the account's own standing credentials are revoked for good. Cancel any time before that with `POST /me/account/deletion/cancel` (a code) or the emailed link; cancelling restores what was paused. post.description: Issue a delegation: your proven domain (the `control_proof`) authorizes an artifact — a package (`purl`) or an https endpoint (`url`) — for a set of capability scopes. Mints a signed delegation token (ES256 — same key and JWKS as proof tokens) carrying `principal`, `delegate`, `scope`, `control_proof` and its own revocation handle. The token is what you publish; the record is what you revoke. A requested lifetime longer than the control proof's remaining one is rejected, never truncated. Each mint consumes 1 proof from your plan quota (re-issuance included).

400.description: `invalid_delegate` (the artifact could not be canonicalized), `invalid_scope` (a scope entry is not a lowercase kebab-case token — an API-style `payments:read` is the common mistake), `control_proof_not_active`, `control_proof_not_domain`, or `delegation_lifetime_exceeds_control_proof`. The code names WHICH input to change. A scope entry longer than 64 characters, more than 32 entries, or an empty array is caught by the request schema BEFORE the controller and answers `validation_error` instead — `invalid_scope` covers the token GRAMMAR

get.description: List YOUR delegations, newest first. There is deliberately no public enumeration over anyone else's delegations — the public read shape is a point lookup of a handle you already hold (`GET /api/v1/proofs/{id}/status` accepts `ph_dlg_*`). Every item carries the DERIVED `effective_status` and `is_valid` beside its stored `status`, the same pair the detail returns: a delegation whose domain control proof was revoked, suspended or expired — or whose OWN lifetime has run out — reports that here even though its own `status` is untouched. Render `effective_status`. Returns 503 `delegation_status_unavailable` if that cascade cannot be resolved — a page is never served with stored statuses standing in for derived ones.

schema.description: Filters the delegation's OWN stored record — whether you revoked it yourself. It deliberately does NOT filter on the derived `effective_status`: that cascade spans two collections and cannot be expressed in the query, and filtering it after the fact would punch holes in both the page and its total. `?status=active` therefore still returns a delegation whose control proof died; read `effective_status` on each item.

A key holding `confirmations:create` without `hitl:read` receives only `public_key` and `kid`: what it needs to seal a confirmation message, nothing more.

put.description: Upload the client-generated RSA keypair for a HITL config. `?force=true` acknowledges the key-rotation cascade, which invalidates envelopes wrapped to the previous key. A ROTATION (a new `kid` on an active config) from a JWT dashboard session requires a live `hitl_key_rotate` 2FA step-up grant (`403 2fa_required` — start one via `POST /me/2fa/start` with `action_type: hitl_key_rotate`); an API-key caller is not step-up gated. Every successful rotation, from either path, emails the account owner at their primary email address (when one is on file). A same-`kid` update (re-wrapping the private key) and the first upload on a config without a keypair need no grant and send no email.

Fired when a verification request passes its `expires_at` without completing. Delivered by the hourly expiry sweep (never on a request read) — at-least-once, including for requests marked expired on read before the sweep ran. A one-shot marker de-duplicates, but rare overlapping sweeps may deliver more than once: dedupe on `request_id`. The payload carries `status: "expired"` and any proofs verified before expiry (an empty array when none were).

Fired by two sources with two body shapes. A HITL confirmation approved on the approval page sends `ConfirmationWebhookPayload` (`confirmation_id`, the stored `message` — see `encrypted` for what it is — and the signed proof of the decision). A verification request created with `action_type: "confirmation"` that completes sends `WebhookPayload` (`request_id`, `action_context`, `proofs`) to its `callback_url`. Tell them apart by `confirmation_id` vs `request_id`.
Fired when a confirmation is denied — by an approver, or by the system (`response.channel` `system`) on a timeout (`response.text` `timeout`), a key rotation or an archived config.

Fired when the recipient of a consent request (an authorization) taps Allow. The authorization is now `active`; an approver who is not the account owner must still complete encryption enrollment before confirmations can be sent to them (`403 approver_not_enrolled` until then).
